content: The studies involving antimalarial medicines were deemed unrelated to the subject of this guideline. It was determined that none of the research projects or appointments had any direct connection to the agenda of the meeting. These declarations were evaluated as non-personal, non-specific, and without any direct or indirect personal or financial benefit, and therefore considered non-significant. Professor Arjen Dondorp disclosed that, starting in February 2021, he has chaired the Malaria Advisory Council of Novartis, a role for which he does not receive remuneration. In 2014, his research group received a grant from Guilin Pharma (now Fosun) to study intravenous artesunate. Currently, his group is investigating the efficacy and safety of triple ACTs (artemisinin-based combination therapies) for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in the context of increasing antimalarial drug resistance. One of the triple ACTs, artemether-lumefantrine-amodiaquine, is provided free of charge by Fosun Pharma. These declarations were assessed as not directly related to the medicines discussed by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and were considered non-personal, non-specific, and non-significant. Professor Marcus Lacerda declared institutional grants from Medicines for Malaria Venture and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation to study the operational feasibility of appropriate Plasmodium vivax radical cure using tafenoquine or primaquine. These interests were assessed as having no direct or indirect personal or financial benefit and were therefore considered non-significant. Professor Terrie Taylor disclosed serving on two advisory boards for Novartis AG and receiving $3,125 in 2019. Her university and research group have received multiple rounds of funding from the United States National Institutes of Health. None of these were directly related to the GDG’s considerations, and it was determined that she could participate in the group’s discussions. These interests were assessed as non-personal and non-specific. The recommendations for interventions in the final phase of malaria elimination and prevention of re-establishment were developed by the Guidelines Development Group, Guidelines Steering Group, and External Review Group, as outlined in the 2022 publication. The groups also included members of the systematic review production and management team, as well as the guidelines methodologist. The final composition of these groups was confirmed at the time of the guideline’s finalization. The recommendations include: Mass drug administration (MDA) to reduce transmission of Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. Mass relapse prevention to reduce transmission of Plasmodium vivax. Members of the Guidelines Development Group (2022) included experts in malaria control, elimination, and transmission, as well as specialists in mathematical modeling and program management. The group was composed of professionals from various countries and institutions, including Dr. Jane Achan (Malaria Consortium, UK), Dr. Mohammed Alzahrani (Ministry of Health, Saudi Arabia), Dr. Kevin Baird (University of Oxford, Indonesia), Professor Teun Bousema (Radboud University, Netherlands), and others. The WHO Secretariat conducted due diligence, including online searches, to identify potential conflicts of interest among GDG members. Relevant declared interests were assessed by the WHO Secretariat with support from the Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. The following declarations were disclosed and managed: Dr. Kevin Baird reported research support for a clinical trial of tafenoquine combined with ACT for radical cure of Plasmodium vivax. This was determined not to conflict with the meeting but was disclosed to GDG members. Professor Teun Bousema reported research funding related to evaluating the impact of MDA and mass testing and treatment (MTaT) on malaria transmission. This was disclosed but not considered a serious conflict. Professor Dionicia Gamboa reported research support from FIND Diagnostics for validating a malaria rapid diagnostic test. This was disclosed but not deemed a serious conflict. Dr. Marcus Lacerda reported research interests in tafenoquine, an 8-aminoquinoline, for radical cure of Plasmodium vivax infections. This was disclosed but not considered a conflict. Dr. Kevin Marsh disclosed advisory roles with WHO, USAID, the Malaria Vaccine Initiative, and PATH. These were disclosed but not considered conflicts. Dr. Kamini Mendis disclosed her role as Director of the Board of the Asia Pacific Leaders Malaria Alliance and authorship of a 2019 paper in the Malaria Journal debating the implementation of MDA. Due to potential bias, she was recused from making judgments on MDA recommendations. Professor Melissa Penny declared financial research support received by her institute related to malaria elimination. This was disclosed but not considered a conflict. Dr. Allan Schapira disclosed his position on the Board of Trustees of the UK-based charity Malaria Consortium. This was disclosed but not considered a conflict. Dr. Chansuda Wongsrichanalai disclosed a paid consultancy with Medicines for Malaria Venture on radical therapy for Plasmodium vivax and travel/per diem support for international meetings. These were disclosed but not considered conflicts. The WHO guidelines for malaria, published on October 16, 2023, provide comprehensive recommendations for malaria control and elimination, supported by systematic reviews and expert input.
